newsitem.title: USA: Dollar falls on post-election profit-taking.
newsitem.headline: Dollar falls on post-election profit-taking.

text.p: NEW YORK, Nov 6 - The dollar fell versus the Japanese yen and German mark on Wednesday as currency traders booked profits after United States election results came in as expected in the financial markets.

Speculation that voters would re-elect Democratic President Bill Clinton but keep the congress controlled by Republicans had boosted the dollar on Tuesday. Confirmation of that outcome prompted traders to dump dollars in what was deemed a classic "buy-on-the-rumour, sell-on-the-news" reaction.
Reports of a sharp increase in Japan's trade surplus and fresh doubts that a single European currency will debut in 1999 as planned also pressured the dollar.

"It was a type of day to see some consolidation, some profit-taking, for the dollar to base and then to try and go higher," said Hillel Waxman, a first vice president of foreign exchange at Bank Leumi Trust Co of New York.

The dollar slid as low as 113.67 yen and 1.5138 marks on Wednesday before partially erasing losses. In late New York trading, the dollar was at 113.95 yen and 1.5175 marks, down from 114.25 yen and 1.5200 marks on Tuesday.

The Ministry of Finance reported that Japan's customs-cleared trade surplus ballooned 22.1 percent in the first 20 days of October from the same period a year earlier but cautioned the increase was only a reaction to last year's rapid decline in exports. The news weighed on the dollar.

"If it (the Japan trade surplus) continues that way, U.S. officials may be concerned about it (and) start talking the dollar down," said Mike Malpede, a senior foreign exchange analyst at Refco Group Ltd.
A weaker dollar might make American-made exports more attractive to foreigners.
Concern about the timely debut of a single European currency arose from rumours and reports released on Wednesday.

Talk circulated in the foreign exchange market that German investment house Deutsche Morgan Grenfell was preparing to tell customers it expected the single currency might be delayed by two-years. The dollar had lost ground to the mark, as the German currency is viewed as a safe haven when ever doubts increase that the single currency will not be launched on time.

Deutsche Morgan senior currency analyst Marc Chandler said the firm feels the risk that European Monetary Union is postponed or scuttled altogether has increased marginally, but the firm still believes the odds favour a small group of countries going ahead with monetary union on schedule.

Separately, the European Monetary Institute released a report stating that a majority of member states do not currently fulfil the necessary conditions for the adoption of a single currency. This stood in contrast to a European Commission report also released on Wednesday that painted a rosy outlook for economic growth next year and saw a vast majority of 12 nations in the European Union meeting the tests for a single currency.
"There's concern that European Monetary Union won't go forward and the money will run back into Germany," Refco's Malpede said.
Elsewhere, the British pound weakened after a Bank of England quarterly report warned about prospects of higher inflation and the risk that the pound's recent strength might prove temporary.
The pound slipped to $1.6415 in late trade on Wednesday from $1.6470 on Tuesday.
The dollar rose slightly to 1.2775 Swiss francs and Canadian $1.3318 from 1.2765 francs and C$1.3305.
